message.content: A world made of angles and color cannot be whole until one small, real creature gives it a center. The abstract world spread in ribbons of blue and yellow, and nothing in it had edges that agreed to stay. A hedgehog named Miso walked through the shifting fields wearing a pair of round glasses, and when he touched a line, the line remembered how to be a line. His nose was dry, his quills were real, and his glasses reflected nothing but himself, because there was no other real thing to reflect. Abstraction is not emptiness, but a way of seeing without names. Miso watched the shapes argue. A triangle became a river, a circle became a laugh, and a smear of red became a door that opened only when he stopped looking. The abstract world had no memory, no hunger, no fear. It had only pattern, and the pattern moved as if it were trying to become something it could not say. The hedgehog with glasses is the only real creature in the abstract world. When the colors asked him what he was, Miso adjusted his glasses and answered, “A small point.” The abstract world turned itself around to hear him. He was the only creature with a heartbeat, the only thing that could blink, the only being whose shadow fell the same way twice. The shapes wanted to be him, but they only became copies of his outline and then scattered. A single real point can make an entire abstract painting feel alive. At the end of the story, the abstract world did not become real. It simply arranged itself around Miso, as a face arranges itself around a pair of glasses. He was still small, still sharp, still the only creature that truly existed, but he was no longer alone. The painting now had a center, and the center had a name: hedgehog.
